questions.question: Which three structural requirements turn a binary operation into a group operation?
options: Commutativity, a determinant, and a basis.
Closure, scalar multiplication, and an inner product.
A zero vector, a norm, and an angle.
Associativity, an identity element, and inverses for every element.

questions.question: In a group, if $ab=ac$, what can you conclude?
options: $b=c$
$a=e$
nothing can be concluded

questions.question: Does a group have to be commutative?
options: No. If it is commutative, it is called Abelian.
No, because groups cannot have binary operations.
Yes. Commutativity is one of the three group axioms.
Yes, but only for matrix groups.

questions.question: How many identity elements can a group have?
options: One per element
Exactly one
At least two
None is required

questions.question: What fails first when trying to make positive natural numbers under addition into a group?
options: Addition is not closed.
Additive inverses are not in the set.
There is no binary operation.
Addition is not associative.

questions.question: Why is $(\mathbb Z,+)$ a group?
options: Only positive integers have inverses, but in fact every integer has one
Addition is associative, $0$ is the identity, and every integer $a$ has inverse $-a$.
The identity element is $1$.
Addition is not closed on integers.

questions.question: Why is $(\mathbb N,+)$ not a group when $\mathbb N$ means positive natural numbers?
options: Most elements lack an additive inverse
Addition is not associative
$1$ is not a natural number.
Addition is not closed.

questions.question: Is $(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\},\cdot)$ a group?
options: No, because multiplication is not associative.
No, because multiplication has no identity.
Yes, every nonzero real number has reciprocal inverse.
No, because $0$ is missing and must be the identity.

questions.question: Why is the set of all $2\times2$ real matrices under multiplication not a group?
options: The product of two $2\times2$ matrices is never $2\times2$.
Matrix multiplication has no identity.
Some matrices are singular and have no inverse.
Matrix multiplication is not associative.

questions.question: Which set is a group under ordinary multiplication?
options: $\mathbb R$ including $0$
$\mathbb N_0$ under multiplication

questions.question: What extra condition makes a group Abelian?
options: Existence of an identity element.
Existence of inverse elements.
Failure of associativity.
Commutativity of the group operation.

questions.question: Why is one noninvertible element enough to disprove that a monoid is a group?
options: A group has no identity element.
A group cannot contain a nonidentity element.
A group requires every element to have an inverse.
A group requires at least one element to lack an inverse.

questions.question: What group axiom is responsible for the fact that equations can often be undone in a group?
options: Commutativity only.
Existence of inverses.
The choice of notation for the operation.
The number of elements in the set.

questions.question: In the additive group $\mathbb Z_5$, what is the inverse of $4$?
Do invertible $2\times2$ real matrices form a group under multiplication?
options: No, because matrix multiplication is not associative.
Yes, this is the group $GL_2(\mathbb R)$.
No, because the identity matrix is not invertible.
No, because products of invertible matrices are singular.

questions.question: Why are real numbers under addition an Abelian group?
options: Addition has no identity.
Addition is associative but no real number has an inverse.
Addition is associative, has identity $0$, has inverses, and is commutative.
Positive and negative real numbers are not closed under addition.

questions.question: In a group, each element $a$ has:
options: an inverse only if the group is abelian
no inverse unless $a=e$
exactly one inverse
possibly several inverses

questions.question: Can a group be noncommutative but still satisfy all group axioms?
options: Yes. Commutativity is not required for groups.
No. Noncommutativity destroys inverses.
Only if the group has exactly one element.
No. Associativity and commutativity are the same axiom.

questions.question: Does $\{1,-1,i,-i\}$ form a group under complex multiplication?
options: Yes, products stay in the set and each element has an inverse there
No, because the identity $1$ is not in the set.
No, because complex multiplication is not associative
No, because $i$ has no inverse.

questions.question: Why is $\{0,1\}$ under multiplication not a group?
options: The product $0\cdot1$ leaves the set.
Multiplication is not associative.
The element $0$ has no multiplicative inverse.
The identity $1$ is missing.
